1:
The two adverbs at the head of the Epistle start a quarrel inside this catena. Chrysostom says flatly that at sundry times and in divers manners are the same as in different ways, and Robertson agrees, calling the pair a sonorous hendiadys for variously and citing him for it. Calvin names him and refuses: some of the fathers, such as Chrysostom, regarded the two words as meaning the same thing, but there is no reason for this, one expressing a variety as to parts and the other as to mode. Calvin then makes the diversity an argument: God would have followed one mode perpetually had it been perfect, so the variety was an evidence of imperfection. Ellicott is after the same contrast from the word order: the fine arrangement of the Authorised Version fails, he says, to convey the emphasis of the original, which he would render, in many portions and in many ways God having of old spoken unto the fathers in the prophets — words that might serve as the motto of the whole Epistle.

What the many ways were, each supplies from his own stock. Gill lists angels, a dream, a vision, and the Urim and Thummim; Henry adds the illapses of the Spirit, an audible voice, and legible characters under God’s own hand when he wrote the ten commandments on stone. On the many portions Henry offers a ladder of gradual discovery: to Adam that the Messiah should come of the seed of the woman, to Abraham that he should spring from his loins, to Jacob that he should be of Judah, to David of his house, to Micah that he should be born at Bethlehem, to Isaiah of a virgin. Wesley dates two, the creation revealed in Adam’s time and the last judgment in Enoch’s, and observes that the very number of the prophets showed they prophesied only in part.

That the revelation is now closed three assert in the same breath. Wesley says the phrase intimates that no other revelation is to be expected, and adds that there were no prophets for a large tract of time before Christ came, that the great Prophet might be the more earnestly expected. Henry says we must expect no new revelation, but only more of the Spirit of Christ to help us understand what is already revealed, the canon being settled and sealed so that men are no longer held in suspense by the expectation of new discoveries. Calvin says it was not a word in part that Christ brought, but the final conclusion. Chrysostom reads the opening as pastoral: the hearers were afflicted and thought themselves worse off than all other men, so the writer shows at the very opening that they had been made partakers of greater grace. And he asks why Paul did not set himself against the prophets, since a greater trust was committed to him, answering that it was to avoid speaking great things of himself, that his hearers were not yet perfect, and that he wished rather to exalt them.

The two longest introductions pull opposite ways. Barnes is anxious: the main object is to prevent defection, the danger being a relapse into the Jewish system, whose imposing rites, public favour, antiquity and undisputed divine origin all tended that way. Clarke is exultant, calling it by far the most important and useful of the apostolic writings, an epitome of the dispensations of God to man, the sum of the Gospel and the completion of the Law, its language pure and elegant as that of the most accomplished Grecian orators, and a work that may be read a hundred times over without any sense of sameness. Robertson notes only that the Epistle begins like Genesis and the Fourth Gospel with God, three relatives carrying the sentence on to present the Son as the exact counterpart of God.
2:
Three of them stop at the missing article. Clarke says it is very remarkable that the pronoun his is not in the text, nor in any manuscript or version, so we should not supply it as our translators have done but read simply, in a Son: God has many sons and many heirs, but no Son who is heir of all things, none by whom he made the worlds, but Jesus the Christ. Ellicott agrees that the rendering surprises but is absolutely needed, since the question answered is not who the Revealer is but what he is, and the contrast with the prophets, who in the lower sense were among God’s sons, proves that one out of many is not meant. Robertson makes the same observation from the grammar: the absence of article and pronoun gives the absolute sense of Son, so the point is not what Jesus said but what he is.

On the phrase about these days, Gill and Ellicott both go to Jewish usage. Gill reports that several copies read in the last of these days, agreeing with the Hebrew phrase, and cites the rule that wherever the last days are mentioned the days of the Messiah are meant, adding that they are the last days not of the natural world but of the Jewish state. Ellicott notes the same oddity, explains that Jewish writers divided time into this world and the coming world, and concludes that every Jewish reader would take the end of these days for the time of Messiah’s appearing. Barnes guards against a different misreading: such phrases do not imply that the world was soon coming to an end, only that this is the last dispensation, which might be longer than all the others put together and still be the last.

Barnes then presses the word us, which need not mean that the writer had heard Christ, or those written to: it may be said with entire propriety that God has spoken to us by his Son though we have neither heard nor seen him, since we have what he spoke and caused to be recorded. He describes the whole process as a dawn — at first a little light, increasing and expanding till objects become visible, and then the sun rising in full-orbed glory.

When the heirship began they cannot agree. Wesley puts it before the creation: God appointed him heir long before he made the worlds, the Son being the firstborn, born before all things, while heir is a term relating to the creation which followed. Calvin puts it at the incarnation, the title ascribed to Christ as manifested in the flesh, since being made man he put on our nature and as such received the heirship, that he might restore what we had lost in Adam. Ellicott rejects the reading Wesley holds, that as Eternal Son he must be Heir of all: that is less consistent with the word appointed, with the strict significance of heir, and with the development of the thought, and what is really expressed is the consummation of all things in the Christ. Clarke sets the verse at the foot of a ten-step climax which begins with the lowest state in which Christ appeared, a Son born of a woman, and ends with his exercising dominion when earth and heaven are no more. On the making of the worlds Robertson notes that the Greek word is ages, used here by metonymy for the universe; Calvin argues from it to eternity, since Christ must have existed before the world was created by him. Cyril presses the word the other way: Christ is Maker not only of the things seen but of the things not seen, thrones and dominions and principalities and powers, and even if you speak of the worlds, of these too he is the Maker at the Father’s bidding.
3:
The image of the sun and its ray does most of the work here. Gill says the allusion is to the sun and its beam, and draws from it that Father and Son are of one nature, neither before the other and not to be divided. Clarke builds propositions on it: Christ is of one essence with the Father, since a proceeding splendour must be of the same essence as the inherent, yet a distinct person, as the splendour of the sun is distinct from the sun; and eternal with the Father, since if the inherent be uncreated the proceeding is. Barnes puts it simply: the sun itself we do not see and its beams we do. Robertson sets out the choice the word offers, reflected brightness or emitted, names Calvin for the first and the Greek fathers for the second, and judges emitted the better fit, though it carries the idea of eternal generation. Ellicott hears the Nicene Creed, Light of Light, and finds the word in the Book of Wisdom, where wisdom is the effulgence of the everlasting light, a parallel Clarke cites too.

Whether the verse describes the eternal Son or the incarnate Mediator divides them. Ellicott says the designations relate to the Son’s essential nature and have no limitation to time; Robertson agrees, calling it absolute and timeless being. Barnes reports that most ancient commentators referred it to his divine dignity before the incarnation, and dissents: it describes him as incarnate, the equal of the Father in human flesh. Calvin holds it is said partly of the divine essence and partly as he is partaker of our flesh, and warns off the question: they who carry their philosophy higher weary themselves and mistake the design of the Apostle, whose object was not to show what likeness the Father bears the Son but to build up our faith, that we may learn God is made known in no other way than in Christ. Chrysostom had said the same far earlier and more starkly: neither tongue nor thought can utter anything suitable to God, and when discourse fails we should then especially glorify him. Lo, we speak, and do not understand, he says: I said that he is everywhere, but I do not understand it; I said that he is without beginning, and understand that no better.

On the express image the metaphor is sealing, and three take it so. Clarke says it is a die leaving the full impression of its every part on the wax; Wesley, that whatever the Father is is exhibited in the Son as a seal in the stamp on wax; Robertson traces the Greek word from the tool that marks to the mark itself. Ellicott alone attacks the English: person is an unfortunate mistranslation here, most earlier versions having substance, and person entering only with a sixteenth-century revision.

The last three clauses are divided among them. On upholding, Clarke says he spake and all things were created, he speaks and all things are sustained; Robertson remarks that the newer science of his day agrees with the personal conception of creation here. On the purging, Ellicott reports that older manuscripts omit by himself and our, leaving simply that he made purification of sins, and holds the shorter reading more majestic; Wesley keeps the phrase and reads it as without Mosaic rites, adding that for this he must for a time divest himself of his glory; Robertson notes the first mention of Christ’s priestly work, the keynote of the Epistle. On the sitting, Wesley gives the best sentence: the priests stood while they ministered, so sitting denotes the consummation of the sacrifice, and the words sat down contain the scope, the theme and the sum of the epistle. Cyril, interested in nothing else here, strings the testimonies to that session out of Matthew, Peter and three of Paul’s letters, ending on this verse.
4:
The participle rendered being made divides them at once. Henry will not have it mean created: the word joined with an adjective is nowhere rendered so, and may be read being more excellent, as one old version has it, on the pattern of let God be true, which means not made so but acknowledged to be so. Gill agrees that Christ was made so only when he was manifested and declared to be so, the phrase signifying no more than that he was. Ellicott takes the other road: better, having become, the words being joined closely to the end of the previous verse, since they speak not of the glory which was ever his but of that which became his after he had made purification of sins. Robertson marks the same contrast in the Greek, a became set against the timeless being of the verse before, and Wesley says plainly that it was by his exaltation, after he had been lower than they.

Why angels need refuting at all four explain the same way. Henry says the apostle forestalls an objection the Jewish zealots would make, that the law was not merely delivered by men but ordained by angels, than whom we know no being higher but God. Calvin says the world is strangely inclined to superstition, so the Jews obscured the glory of God by extolling angels too much, and it was necessary to reduce them to their own rank lest they overshadow the brightness of Christ. Clarke supplies the evidence, that the Jews associated angels with God in the creation and allowed them to be worshipped for their Creator’s sake though not for their own; then he turns their own ground against them in a syllogism, that he who is greater than the angels and is the object of their adoration is God, and Jesus Christ is both.

Whether he holds the name by inheritance is disputed by two who agree about everything else. Wesley says that because he is the Son of God he inherits the name, in right whereof he inherits all things, and dates the two: his inheriting the name more ancient than all worlds, his inheriting all things as ancient as all things. Clarke denies the word outright: it is not by inheritance that Christ possesses a more excellent name but as God, having it naturally and essentially. Robertson notes only that the perfect means he inherited and still inherits it; Barnes gives the domestic figure, a son having rank in a family above servants, angels being the servants of God and of the church.

What the name is they mostly agree; what name means, they do not. Barnes says the title is Son, and that although angels and saints are called sons of God in general, the title the Son of God has been given to him only. Ellicott says it covers all the dignity contained in the name, which did not first belong to him as exalted Mediator, the glory that became his being proportionate to a name his by essential right. Robertson glosses name in the oriental sense of rank — exactly the reading Calvin rejects, who says that some by name understand dignity, but not correctly, as appears from what follows, for the name is that of a Son. Ellicott then asks whether the coming quotations are meant as strict demonstration, and answers that they address men who already believed the Christ had appeared in Jesus, so that the object is less to convince of a new truth than to show what the well-known passages really contain. Wesley alone notices the shape of the argument: the verse has two clauses, the second taken up at once and the first not until the end of the chapter, a transposition the Jewish doctors were fond of and the apostle adopts in becoming all things to all men.
5:
When this day was they cannot settle. Clarke holds the words must refer either to the incarnation or to the resurrection and decides for the resurrection, on which he builds: the rising proves Christ innocent, since God could not raise a wicked man by miracle, proves the conception miraculous, and vindicates his mother. Wesley answers with eternity: I have begotten thee from eternity, which by its unalterable permanency is one continued, unsuccessive day. Ellicott holds both. Paul refers the words to the Resurrection, he grants, and that agrees with the previous verse; but since the exaltation there answers to an essential dignity already lying in the name Son, we are constrained to regard the day of the Resurrection as itself typical, pointing also to the eternal Now, the day co-extensive with the unbegotten and everlasting life of God. Robertson only reports the division.

The objection that others too are called sons of God is raised and answered by three. Calvin puts it hardest against himself: princes are called gods and sons of the Most High, Israel God’s firstborn, and David himself calls angels the sons of God. The answer, he says, is in no way difficult: princes are so called on a particular occasion, Israel by the grace of election, angels as celestial spirits resembling God in their blessed immortality; but when David, as the type of Christ, calls himself the Son of God without addition, he denotes something peculiar, and stands apart from all other beings. Ellicott says the inferior use does not affect the argument, since every reader must perceive that Son is here used of One and in a unique sense. Robertson sharpens it to a word: to which individual angel? As a class angels are called sons of God, but no single angel is ever called God’s Son as the Messiah is. Gill says only that God never said to any of them what he said to Christ.

That the words had an earlier owner none denies. Calvin says it cannot be denied that this was spoken of David as he sustained the person of Christ: David enlarged his borders, some foreshadowing of the heathen given for an inheritance, but how little beside a kingdom reaching from east to west, his glory hardly a spark to Christ’s. Ellicott is more exact, giving their first sense as, I have this day established thee as my chosen king and so made thee my son, and saying the second passage is not a direct prophecy of Christ but belonged first to an earthly ruler. Wesley concedes the same in a clause: it related immediately to Solomon, but in a far higher sense to the Messiah.

Barnes admits a difficulty the others pass over: applying these passages to the Messiah raises a difficulty not easy to explain. His defence is historical rather than exegetical. It is to be presumed they were applied to the Messiah in Paul’s time, that his readers would admit it, and that he did not expect it to be questioned; then Barnes generalises. Every age and people have their own modes of reasoning, he says, which may strike others as unsound and yet be conclusive to that age; the ancient philosophers reasoned in ways we should not think tenable, and so it is with the Chinese, the Hindoos, the Mohammedans now; in a writer of any age we are to expect the prevailing mode, and where he reasons with an adversary, the points that adversary concedes. And this, Barnes says, is not wrong. Cyril is the one voice still arguing with that adversary: the Jews admit one God but not that he is the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, and think to be made friends of the Father apart from devotion to the Son; but he that refuses the Way and denies the Door, how shall he be deemed worthy of entrance unto God?
6:
What again attaches to, and when the bringing in happened, produces six answers. Barnes says again refers not to a second bringing but to the course of the argument, meaning in another place. Ellicott says the word's position in the Greek shows the opposite, that it must join with leadeth, and reads a second leading in for judgment. Clarke calls the rendering incorrect and translates, when he bringeth again, or the second time, the firstborn into the habitable world, referring it to the resurrection, which might properly be called a second incarnation; and he presses the noun, the first coming being described by a word for the globe and this by a word for the inhabited earth, because now he was to dwell with man. Gill also takes it of the second coming, as agreeable to the natural order of the words; Wesley takes it flatly of the incarnation. Robertson lays out both options, the Second Coming if again goes with the verb and the incarnation if it merely introduces another quotation, and says there is no way to decide certainly.

Chrysostom is interested in the direction of the movement, not its date. Christ calls his coming in the flesh a going out and Paul a coming in, and both are just: a going out, because we were outside, as prisoners who have offended the king stand without the palace, and he who would reconcile them goes out himself and talks with them until they are fit for the king’s presence; a coming in, from the metaphor of those who enter on an inheritance, the phrase meaning, when he putteth the world into his hand.

The quotation itself has no Hebrew original, and three say so. Barnes finds the words in the Greek at the end of the Song of Moses but not in the Hebrew, nor in all copies of the Greek. Clarke reports that some send us to a psalm instead, but the Messiah is not clearly intended there and the words are not precisely these, whereas in the Song they stand word for word, with nothing answering in the Hebrew. Calvin cites the psalm without noticing any difficulty, and meets a different objection, that it seems unreasonable to apply to Christ what is spoken of God only: to answer that Christ is the eternal God would avail little in a doubtful point, so he argues that the whole psalm is about Christ’s kingdom. Clarke draws the sharper inference: to worship a creature is idolatry, so if Christ were a creature the angels commanded to worship him would be idolaters and God the author of their idolatry.

Whether the next verse says spirits or winds divides them again. Ellicott says winds, since the ordinary rendering yields no clear meaning and the parallelism is complete, angels answering to ministers and winds to a flame of fire; and against the proposal to invert the clause, so that God makes winds his messengers, he records a decided opinion that his own rendering gives the Hebrew and suits the psalm. Barnes leans the other way, allowing the inverted sense is perhaps what would most naturally occur to a reader of the Hebrew. Calvin goes furthest: David is describing how the world is governed, nothing is more certain than that the winds are meant, and this has nothing to do with angels; the Apostle argues by likeness, the winds performing offices below such as angels perform above, being as it were visible spirits. Robertson concedes the Hebrew and denies its relevance: the inversion is true, but not the point here. Cyril, placed here by that word, warns against the very confusion the others fell into: many things are called spirit, an angel, our soul, the wind that is blowing, great virtue, impure practice, the devil our adversary; so beware, lest from their having a common name thou mistake one for another.
8:
Everything turns on whether the Greek is a vocative. Clarke reports that some later versions render it God is thy throne for ever and ever, and grants that if that is right the text proves nothing; then he answers. The nominative form is often used for the vocative, particularly by the Attics; the scope of the place requires it; the Hebrew admits no other rendering; and even allowing the nominative, the sense contended for needs a verb supplied which no version and no manuscript yet discovered countenances. Calvin calls the alternatives mere evasions, made lest Christ be owned as God, and says whoever reads the verse with a sound mind and free from the spirit of contention cannot doubt that the Messiah is here called God; nor may it be objected that the word is sometimes used of angels and judges, since it is never given simply to one person except to God alone. Wesley compresses the argument into a line: God in the singular number is never used in scripture absolutely of any but the supreme God. Robertson leaves the door the others are shutting: it is not certain whether the word is vocative or nominative with is understood, and either makes good sense.

Whether the psalm was ever about Solomon divides them as sharply. Barnes will not have it at all: he sees not why the psalm should ever have been supposed applicable to Solomon, whose name is not mentioned and to whom nothing in it peculiarly belongs, since the king described is a conqueror, girding his sword on his thigh, his arrows sharp in the hearts of his foes, while Solomon’s was a reign of peace, nor was he ever distinguished for war. It had, he concludes, an original and exclusive reference to the Messiah, the hero of the Old Testament more than Achilles is of the Iliad. Ellicott answers that view directly, finding insuperable objections to taking the psalm as altogether prophetic and holding it written for the marriage of some king of David’s line, and adding that many of the arguments urged against a reference to Solomon have no great weight: the Psalmist uses words which bear their full meaning only of that Son of David whose kingdom shall have no end. Calvin takes the middle: the psalm was composed as a marriage song for Solomon, but what is related is much too high to be applied to him. Robertson calls it a Hebrew nuptial ode treated here as Messianic.

On the reception they agree. Barnes says the application has been generally admitted by Jewish and Christian interpreters; Clarke cites a rabbi who says the psalm speaks of David, or rather of his son the Messiah; Ellicott infers that the readers of the Epistle would recognise the argument at once. He alone looks at the manuscripts, the two oldest Greek copies reading his kingdom at the close of the verse.

The sceptre is left mostly to two. Calvin finds obscure lineaments of a righteous reign in Solomon, but says righteousness in Christ’s kingdom is wider, since by his gospel, which is his spiritual sceptre, he renews us after the righteousness of God, and makes it reign in his own people because he loves it. Robertson notes only that the word is an old one for a walking-stick. Gill takes the verse as saying what is never said to angels, showing him a Prince and not a minister, and ascribing deity to him. Cyril turns from the throne to the anointing and then to his hearers: Christ was anointed not by men with material ointment but by the Father with the Holy Ghost; and as Christ was in reality crucified and raised, and you in Baptism are accounted worthy of being crucified and raised with him in a likeness, so is it with the unction, you being anointed as partakers and fellows of Christ.
9:
Who the fellows are gets four answers. Clarke takes them for all who ever held the anointed offices: none was ever constituted prophet, priest and king but Christ, some being kings only, some prophets only, some two of the three, none all three in his own person; and he reports the other reading, that fellows means believers partaking of the same Spirit, only to prefer the first. Calvin holds the reading Clarke sets aside: Christ was anointed above us all beyond measure while each of us has a limited portion, so that he is the Christ and we Christians proceeding from him as a rivulet from a fountain; Cyril says the same to his hearers, that they were anointed as partakers and fellows of Christ. Ellicott takes them for other earthly kings, Barnes for all who sustain the kingly office, reporting without preferring a suggestion that angels are meant; Wesley makes them all the children of men.

What kind of anointing it was divides them too. Clarke and Barnes read a consecration, kings and priests and prophets being set apart by oil, and Barnes hears in the oil of gladness the perfumed oil poured on the head amid rejoicing, a Messiah’s inauguration being a triumph like a coronation. Calvin prefers a different custom, not the anointing of consecration but that of refreshment offered to guests, the word gladness favouring it, since Christ is addressed as already on his throne; Robertson allows the same. On the words therefore God, even thy God, Barnes says the inserted even weakens the force and it might be rendered, O God, thy God hath anointed thee, naming Clarke among those who so render it; Clarke allows it but is content with the plainer reading; Ellicott calls it possible but not probable.

The second quotation raises the hardest problem in the chapter, since the psalm it comes from is addressed to Jehovah as Creator, and three meet it head on. Barnes argues from relevance: why, in an argument designed to prove the Son superior to the angels, should the writer break out in an address to Jehovah? Such is not the manner of Paul, or of any other good writer. He grants that few reading the psalm would suppose it referred to the Messiah, and turns that into the proof: if none would doubt it referred to God, the apostle’s applying it to the Lord Jesus proves most conclusively that he is divine. Ellicott states the difficulty as plainly and answers from the psalm’s theme, that the Lord shall appear to build up Zion, a hope inseparable from the Messianic promise, so that a Christian Jew who saw it fulfilled in Jesus would recognise the application at once. Calvin allows that Christ is nowhere named in the psalm and yet is so pointed out that none can doubt his kingdom is there recommended, since in vain shall we seek elsewhere than in Christ that God through whom the whole world has been united in one faith. Robertson supplies the fact that complicates all three: the word Lord, on which the address turns, stands in the Greek version and not in the Hebrew.

The creation clause turns on eternity. Gill makes the founding of the earth show it the lower part of the creation and denote stability, and takes the clause to prove the eternity of Christ and confute the notion of an eternal world. Robertson notes the emphatic position of the pronoun. Cyril, whose subject is the Father, arrives at the same greatness from the other end: he is not circumscribed in any place nor less than the heaven, the whole earth being held in his grasp; think not the sun brighter than he, for he who formed the sun must needs be incomparably greater, foreknowing what shall be and subject to no necessary sequence of events, nor to nativity, nor chance, nor fate.
11:
How far the heavens perish is a question of degree. Gill says not as to their substance but as to their quality, the form and fashion passing and the curse removed, the substance continuing, since otherwise there would be no place for the righteous or the wicked; Clarke says the same, that they are changed and renewed, not destroyed ultimately or annihilated. Barnes will not close the question: probably no more is meant than that important changes will take place, yet we cannot foresee what may come in the heavenly bodies, or say that the present universe may not at some period be destroyed and succeeded by a creation still more magnificent. He then asks whether it is absurd to suppose that the sun, which daily sends forth so many countless millions of beams, may in a course of ages be diminished in splendour and shine with feeble lustre. Robertson, a century later, records the answer: modern scientists no longer postulate the eternal existence of the heavenly bodies. Cyril gives a moral reason rather than a physical one: since corruption and theft and adultery have been poured over the earth, and blood mingled with blood, this wondrous dwelling-place must not remain filled with iniquity, so the world passes away that the fairer world may be made manifest.

Clarke turns aside into English: our word world, he says, is a contraction of wear old, a term by which our ancestors expressed the very sentiment of this verse, the older spellings being weorold and wereld; Barnes stays with the same family of words more soberly: wax is an old Saxon word meaning to grow or become.

The folding of the vesture is glossed alike. Gill has clothes grown old or out of fashion folded up and laid aside, and notes that the Hebrew reads, as a vesture shalt thou change them. Ellicott renders it, as a mantle shalt thou roll them up; Wesley adds the words that matter, with all ease. From the immutability that follows Barnes draws his conclusion: what could more clearly prove the speaker immutable, and since it is indubitably spoken of the Messiah it must demonstrate that he is divine, such attributes not being conferrable on a creature. Clarke says the same of the years that shall not fail: in the divine duration there is no circle to be run, no space to be measured, no time to be reckoned, but all is eternity, infinite and onward.

On the last quotation Calvin argues that it can be explained of none but Christ. It was not lawful for kings to touch the priesthood, as the leprosy of Uzziah testifies, and neither David nor any successor of his was ordained a priest; so a new kingdom and a new priesthood are introduced here, the same person being made king and priest, and the eternity of the priesthood suits Christ alone. Ellicott, who has twice refused to read a psalm as purely predictive, allows it of this one: most probably it stands alone among the Psalms as simply prophetic, its words never having been addressed to angels or to an earthly king. Calvin then makes the promise pastoral: were we to regard things as they appear, the kingdom of Christ would often seem on the verge of ruin, but two things must be borne in mind, that it shall never in this world be at rest, and that its enemies shall never prevail. Barnes explains the footstool from the custom of ancient warriors, who stood on the necks of vanquished kings when celebrating a triumph, angels serving as mere instruments in that subduing. Clarke draws the conclusion the chapter has been driving at: the Son is the supreme and absolute Sovereign, they no more than his messengers and servants, and servants even to his servants, that is, to mankind. Cyril, returning to his chain of testimonies, ends where the argument began.
14:
The phrase is placed before it is argued from. Gill says it is Rabbinical, the angels of ministry being the common Jewish appellation, so the apostle, writing to Jews, uses a phrase well known to them. Clarke notes the idiom, since the Hebrews often express the strongest affirmative by an interrogation, so the sense is, they are all ministering spirits. Barnes and Ellicott both trace the Greek word to public service, Barnes to the word from which our liturgy comes, used of those engaged in the temple, Ellicott to those who stood before God in his earthly sanctuary, the word being fitly transferred to the nobler offices of the unseen world.

Whom the angels actually serve is the real question, and it is settled four ways. Barnes says plainly that they render aid to Christians. Ellicott says it may seem to the English reader that those who were God’s ministers a few verses earlier are here made servants of man, and denies it: the words mean sent forth, continually sent forth, to do service to God, for the sake of them who are to inherit salvation. Calvin separates the two Greek words, an official appointment and the work to be done, and renders it, sent forth for service, on account of those who are to inherit salvation. Wesley cuts the knot in six words: ministering before God, sent forth to men.

Whether it is fitting that angels help at all is argued at length by Barnes. There is nothing absurd in it, he says, since it is no more improbable that angels should aid man than that one man should aid another, and it is a great principle of the divine administration that one class of creatures should minister to another, parents to children, the rich to the poor. Then he finds a symmetry: as man was ruined by the temptation of one of an angelic though fallen nature, there is a beautiful propriety in aid coming from the race that brought the ruin, angelic might with heavenly benevolence repairing what fallen brethren inflicted. Clarke says the same in a sentence, that if God help man by man we need not wonder that he helps man by angels, though he needs no such helps; and he grants that what the services are and how performed it would be impossible to state, much having been written partly from Scripture and partly from conjecture.

Calvin takes the comfort, then fences it. It is no common pledge of God’s love that celestial hosts are continually engaged in our behalf, so that our salvation, defended by such guardians, is beyond the reach of danger; but the benefit is granted especially to his chosen, and if angels are to minister to us we must be members of Christ, since, banished by sin from God’s kingdom, we can have no communion with them except through Christ’s reconciliation. He meets the objection from the angels of the Persians and the Greeks in Daniel by answering that their victories always had reference to the benefit of the Church. Robertson fences it differently, denying that the verse gives us guardian angels for each of us and allowing only that angels are used for our good, then quoting a physicist of his own day asking whether we may not be guided by helpers who are agents, like ourselves, of the immanent God. Wesley attaches a condition none of the others does: those who inherit are those who have patiently continued in welldoing. Clarke closes by recommending a sermon of Wesley’s on this very text, and complaining that another commentator’s treatment is learned and judicious but by far too diffuse, the words of God being drowned in the sayings of man. Ellicott ends the chapter where it was always going: it has been occupied throughout with promises of the Christ, and its last word brings before us Jesus, the Saviour.
